disease_info: Bulimia nervosa is characterized by recurrent episodes of eating unusually large amounts of food accompanied by a sense of loss of control, followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives/diuretics, fasting, or excessive exercise to prevent weight gain. Self-evaluation is excessively and often exclusively influenced by body shape and weight, but individuals are typically within normal weight or overweight ranges, which helps distinguish bulimia from anorexia nervosa. The course is often chronic or relapsing, with symptoms waxing and waning in relation to stress, interpersonal difficulties, or changes in weight and self-esteem. It is important to differentiate bulimia from binge-eating disorder, in which compensatory behaviors are absent, and from normative overeating, which lacks the recurrent loss of control and extreme weight/shape overvaluation.

narrative.personality: Horace is a sociable, story-telling retiree who prides himself on being organized, helpful to others, and actively engaged in his community and garden projects.
narrative.stressor: About seven months ago, Horace’s primary care doctor warned him that recent weight gain, elevated blood pressure, and borderline blood sugar put him at higher risk for serious illness, and suggested he tighten his diet. Already sensitive about aging and wanting to keep up with younger volunteers on hikes and garden projects, he became increasingly preoccupied with how his body looked and what others might think when he struggled with stamina or clothes feeling tighter. He started oscillating between strict dieting before social events and then eating large amounts at home afterward when he felt he had “blown it,” gradually developing rigid private rituals around food and ways he believed would quickly “undo” what he had eaten. Over several months, this hidden battle with eating and intense self-criticism about his appearance left him more fatigued and anxious, and he finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after a nurse at the senior center noticed his distress and he admitted he was ashamed of how much his weight and shape had come to dominate his self-worth.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m embarrassed how much my weight and shape are all I think about now, like it’s the only way I judge myself.”

narrative.personality: Gino is a meticulous, competitive retail veteran who channels his anxiety into perfectionistic attention to detail and solitary creative pursuits like painting and woodworking.
narrative.stressor: Roughly seven months ago, Gino’s store brought in a much younger, fit regional manager who emphasized a “sleek, on-brand” staff image and began making comments about tightening uniforms and looking more energetic on the sales floor. Already prone to worrying over small details, Gino started fixating on how his body appeared next to his younger colleagues and how customers might judge an older, heavier salesperson in a visually focused home décor environment. In response, he began cycling between strict self-imposed food rules during the workday and episodes of eating large amounts alone at night when he felt he had failed his own standards, then resorting to increasingly desperate measures afterward to feel like he had erased the damage and could still “look the part” at work. As his preoccupation with weight and shape intensified and began to overshadow his enjoyment of art, woodworking, and even his relationship with his spouse, he sought psychiatric help at his wife’s urging after she found him distressed in the bathroom and he admitted he felt his entire value at work now hinged on how his body looked.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I feel like my whole sense of worth at work depends on how thin I look, and it’s gotten completely out of hand.”

narrative.personality: Jairo is a friendly, bilingual sales associate who mixes a structured work ethic with a laid-back, procrastinating style in his personal life and a love for cooking, gaming, and casual self-improvement projects.
narrative.stressor: Seven months ago, Jairo went through a painful breakup after his partner made repeated digs about his eating habits and joked about him getting a “soft gamer body,” comments that stuck with him more than he expected. Around the same time, a few coworkers started a fitness challenge and shared progress photos in a group chat, and Jairo found himself obsessively comparing his body to theirs and feeling ashamed after family gatherings centered on rich Mexican food he loved to cook. He began alternating between periods of strict control and late-night overeating when he felt lonely or frustrated, then experimenting with ways to quickly get rid of what he had eaten so he wouldn’t “wear it” the next day, a pattern that slowly turned into a secret routine he felt compelled to repeat. As his thoughts about weight and shape became increasingly harsh and he noticed himself avoiding social events and cultural gatherings he once enjoyed, he finally reached out for psychiatric help after a cousin, worried by his frequent bathroom trips after meals, urged him to talk to someone about how far he was going to try to control his body.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve started making myself throw up after I eat because I’m terrified of gaining weight, and I don’t know how to stop.”
